overview: Rapa Nui's archaeological landscape combines sculpture, ceremonial platforms, homes and productive spaces. The living Rapa Nui people must remain visible alongside the famous monuments.

items.text: Moai represent ancestors. Sculptors shaped many from volcanic tuff using harder basalt tools.
Ahu ceremonial platforms combine worked-stone facings and rubble fill, with forecourts and access ramps. Quarries preserve stages of statue production.
Rock paintings and petroglyphs record varied motifs and techniques. Orongo is an important ceremonial village with distinctive stone houses.
Housing, agriculture and production structures are part of the archaeological record. Research should examine them alongside monumental sculpture.
Descendants of earlier Rapa Nui communities live on the island today. Colonial violence, disease and slavery belong in its history without being turned into a story of cultural disappearance.

Rapanui cultivators added stone to gardens to conserve moisture, moderate temperature and improve soils. Different arrangements included surface stones, crushed rock mixed into soil and larger boulders.

A satellite study published in 2024 estimated less rock gardening than earlier surveys and challenged one basis for population-collapse stories. The authors caution that some gardens have disappeared and surviving fields were not necessarily used simultaneously.
